mac-session-check-cache: Every Mac capture and pointer check read the session dictionary and the display geometry from WindowServer, about 48 µs each, several hundred times a second while someone watched. Capture and the pointer now reuse a check that passed within the last 16 ms; a failure is never reused, a display mode change clears it, and input, mode changes and stills always check afresh.
mac-wake-display: ScreenCaptureKit delivers no picture from a sleeping display, and input is admitted only for a recent picture, so a viewer of a Mac whose display had slept saw nothing and could not wake it. A capture that starts or resumes, or finds no picture, now wakes a sleeping display when the Mac is unlocked (declaring user activity, as caffeinate -u does), skipping a closed lid's built-in display, and gives the declaration back when capture stops.
mac-vt-submit-thread: VTCompressionSessionEncodeFrame runs synchronously at 16-aligned sizes, 5 ms at 1920x1200 and 14-15 ms at 4K on an M6, and thread C sat in it while input waited. Each encoder now has a submit thread that makes every VideoToolbox call, fed through a one-slot mailbox; a submit that finds it busy leaves the tick armed, and at most two units are in flight. Handing a picture over now takes microseconds.
mac-vt-rate-control: VideoToolbox's low-latency rate control dropped many frames on full-motion content, and when the dropped picture was the last change the viewer kept the previous one until the 250 ms liveness repeat. Low-latency sessions now allow QP up to 51, and a dropped newest picture is sent again at the next tick, at most twice. Standard rate control for H.265 at high rates and a timestamp rate-model start were measured and not adopted; the record has why.
mac-capture-cadence: ScreenCaptureKit's minimum frame interval was 0.9 / max_fps whatever the display's refresh, so a 144 Hz Mac delivered 48 frames a second to a 60 fps viewer and 72 to a 120 fps one. The interval now admits every n-th refresh, n the pace's multiple of the refresh, read from the display mode or its display link; a pause and a slower pace slow the stream within that bound, a start no longer enumerates every window, a sub-pixel aspect mismatch no longer leaves a dark edge row, and a change of frame-rate limits retunes the stream instead of rebuilding capture and the encoder.
win-mf-output-events: Thread C polled the Media Foundation encoder every 2 ms while a unit was inside, so each unit reached it up to 2 ms late, and an encoder that asks for input only after its last output halved the frame rate when an encode took more than a period. A watcher thread now waits for the MFT's events and wakes thread C for each output and each input request, and a tick whose encoder has not asked for input yet stays armed. An MFT without IMFShutdown keeps the 2 ms drain.
win-encoder-settings: Windows hosts encoded H.264 as Baseline with CAVLC. They now ask the Media Foundation encoder for High with CABAC, rewriting the SPS so it promises no frame reordering, and fall back to Baseline for the rest of the worker when a High encoder fails or emits B-frames. QualityVsSpeed and the display-remoting scenario are read back and logged for device runs to choose by, and the encoder asks for a raised GPU scheduling priority, so capture and conversion queue less behind a full-screen 3D load.
win-capture-convert: Each new picture was copied full-size before the video processor converted it, a rotated display could not be shared at all, and an odd-sized desktop that needed no scaling was resampled by 0.999. The video processor now reads the duplication surface directly, falling back to the copy where a driver refuses; a rotated display is captured and turned upright; an odd edge is cropped instead of scaled; and downscaling asks for quality rather than speed.
win-present-waiter: After stillness, the first change on a Windows desktop waited for thread C's next poll of DXGI, up to a frame period. In process, DXGI is now a push source: a capture thread that thread C arms when its tick finds nothing waits in AcquireNextFrame for the next present, converts it at once and wakes thread C. The helper path keeps polling until the helper can push.
win-hdr-desktop: With Windows HDR or Auto Color Management on, DXGI handed over an FP16 desktop converted without the display's SDR white level, so the shared picture's brightness and mid-tones differed from the local view. FP16 desktops are now drawn on the GPU at the display's SDR white, as the local display shows them; brighter highlights are brought down to white with their hue kept.
win-still-refinement: An encoder that budgets per frame refines a still picture only by one frame's budget per 250 ms liveness repeat, so dense text took seconds to sharpen after a scroll stopped. A Windows encoder can now send a short burst of repeats at the capture pace once a budget-limited picture stops changing, ending when the units become small, the QP stops falling or a limit is reached, without spending the capture tick. It runs only on encoders a device run has listed, and none are listed yet; VideoToolbox gets no burst, since it brought nothing there.
helper-probe-cache: Each privileged Windows session ran in a fresh helper worker that probed H.265 cold before it answered, 320-950 ms that the viewer waited for. The host process now keeps the worker's H.265 answer per adapter and driver for later sessions and forgets it when H.265 fails. Helper protocol 11 (.v11 pipes) carries the adapter, so the desktop service needs Update.
viewer-feedback: Every congestion signal was a round trip, so a queue on the viewer's upload (a backup, a video call, a cellular uplink) cut a healthy forward link. A viewer that lists arrival_time now stamps each receipt and probe echo with when it read the unit, and the host splits the round trip into the queue toward the viewer and the one back; a viewer that lists keyframe_seq names the last unit it read in a keyframe request, so the host skips units the viewer would discard. The quality panel shows both queues; older peers keep round trips.
receipt-rate-control: Congestion cost frame rate first: on a 1 Mbit/s limit the pace fell to 10 FPS while bits per frame barely moved. Receipts now drive rate control: a standing queue cuts bits per frame within a round trip, to the delivery rate the receipts show, while the frame rate holds; only at the preset's floor does the pace fall. In the 1 Mbit/s case the lowest pace rose from 10 to 43-45 FPS and the queue fell from 128-184 ms to 2-11 ms; the bitrate climbs back over 4-5 s after the limit lifts, where it took 1-2 s.
reconnect-start-rate: Reconnects happen most on slow links, yet each new session started at the preset's starting bits per frame, so its first keyframe queued behind the link it had just lost. A viewer that reconnects to the same running host now starts at the rate its previous session closed at; the host keeps that rate, not the room, so it survives the room closing with its last viewer.
pointer-cadence: Hover feedback from the controller's own move waited for the 16 ms cursor clock, other pointers were read at 62.5 Hz even in a 120 FPS session, and every hover forced a full-window Flutter frame over a still picture. The host now reads the pointer at the session's rate (8.3 ms at 120 FPS) and looks for a new shape 2 ms after an injected move, and the viewers repaint the cursor layer only when it draws something different.
mac-viewer-layer: The Mac viewer decodes to BGRA and hands Flutter a texture, so each picture waits for Flutter's next frame. A presenter that shows each decoded 420v picture on a Core Animation layer from the decoder thread, skipping VideoToolbox's BGRA pass and Flutter's frame, is added behind --dart-define=presenter=layer; it becomes the default once its decode-to-glass measurement runs on a lit display.
linux-presenting-gpu: On a hybrid laptop or a desktop with two GPUs, the Linux viewer picked whichever hardware decoder ranked highest, which could keep a sleeping NVIDIA GPU awake for the session and send every picture across PCIe and back. Decoders now run on the GPU that draws the window, read from Flutter's EGL display and sysfs, without waking another GPU to find out.
